concepts.name: Traffic estimates and cost per conversation
RAG, tools and handoff to humans

questions.prompt: A support agent handles 10,000 conversations a day. Each conversation makes 5 model calls, and peak traffic is 5× the daily average. Roughly how many model calls per second must you handle at peak?

choices.text: About 0.1 per second
About 30 per second
About 3 per second
About 580 per second

questions.explanation: 10,000 × 5 = 50,000 calls a day. A day has 86,400 seconds, so the average is about 0.58 calls per second, and 5× that is about 2.9, so about 3 per second. 0.1 is conversations (not calls) per second at average load; 580 is off by a factor of 1,000. The point for the interview: this is modest traffic, and the real constraints are cost, latency per call and provider rate limits.

questions.prompt: Each conversation makes 5 calls of 3,000 input and 250 output tokens. At a hypothetical $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, what is the cost per conversation and per day at 10,000 conversations?

choices.text: About $0.021 per conversation, about $212 a day
About $0.21 per conversation, about $2,125 a day
About $0.015 per conversation, about $150 a day
About $0.0021 per conversation, about $21 a day

questions.explanation: Input: 5 × 3,000 = 15,000 tokens × $1/M = $0.015. Output: 5 × 250 = 1,250 tokens × $5/M = $0.00625. Total about $0.021 per conversation, and × 10,000 = about $212.50 a day. Option c counts input only. Always show the arithmetic out loud; interviewers care more about the method than the prices.

questions.prompt: In a support-agent design interview you're asked: "What does one conversation cost, and how would you bring it down?" Explain how you'd estimate it and which levers you'd pull.

model_answer.summary: Multiply calls per conversation by tokens per call and prices, noting that input usually dominates because each call resends the history and retrieved context; then cut it with caching, routing and trimming.
key_points: Cost per conversation = sum over calls of input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price
Input grows each turn because the whole history, system prompt and retrieved chunks are sent again, so input usually dominates
Prompt caching of the stable prefix (tools and system prompt) cuts the cost of repeated input
Routing simple intents to a smaller model, and escalating only when needed, cuts the price per call
Trimming old turns and sending fewer retrieved chunks cuts tokens per call; eval results confirm quality holds

questions.explanation: A strong answer ties each lever to the part of the formula it changes. Chip Huyen's platform post covers the prompt cache and routing to cheaper models; Week 12's cost-optimisation Lesson covers the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A customer asks two questions: "What is your refund policy?" and "Where is my order #1234?" How should the agent get what it needs for each?

choices.text: Both through RAG over the help centre, which should include recent orders
Refund policy by RAG over help-centre articles; order status by calling an order-lookup tool
Refund policy by an order-lookup tool; order status by RAG over past tickets
Both from the model's own knowledge, fine-tuned on last year's tickets

questions.explanation: Stable, shared knowledge such as policies suits retrieval over documents. Live, per-customer data such as an order's status must come from the system of record through a tool call, because it changes by the minute and belongs to one customer. Anthropic describes support agents exactly this way: tools pull customer data and order history, plus knowledge base articles.

questions.prompt: Which is the best set of triggers for handing a conversation to a human agent?

choices.text: Never hand off; escalating means the agent failed, and full automation is the goal
Hand off after a fixed 20 turns, since long conversations are the ones that go wrong
Whenever the model's reply sounds unsure or hedged, since a hedging tone reliably signals a wrong answer
The customer asks for a person, the action is high-impact (a large refund), or checks keep failing

questions.explanation: Handoff should follow clear rules: an explicit request, actions whose impact needs human approval (OWASP recommends a human approve high-impact actions), or repeated failures such as no grounded answer or output checks failing. Chip Huyen lists human handoff as one way to manage output-guardrail failures. Pass the conversation and a summary along so the customer doesn't repeat themselves.

questions.prompt: Explain how retrieval, tools and human handoff divide the work in your support agent design, and where guardrails sit.

model_answer.summary: Retrieval supplies policy and how-to knowledge, tools read and change per-customer data, and humans take over when rules say so; guardrails check inputs and outputs around the model.
key_points: RAG over help-centre articles and policies answers general questions, with answers grounded in retrieved text
Tools read live customer data (orders, account status) and perform actions such as creating a ticket or issuing a small refund
Tools act with the customer's own permissions, and high-impact actions need human approval
Handoff to a human happens on request, for high-impact cases, or after repeated failures, with a summary passed along
Input guardrails (such as detecting sensitive data or off-topic requests) and output guardrails (such as checking for unsupported claims or malformed replies) wrap the model calls

questions.explanation: This is the core of the design. Interviewers look for the split between static knowledge and live data, for permission limits on tools, and for a defined path to a human. Applied-llms.org's advice to add guardrails rather than trust the model alone applies directly.

questions.prompt: Before launching the support agent, where should your first eval cases come from?

choices.text: Real anonymised support tickets and transcripts, each with assertions a good reply must meet
A public general-knowledge benchmark, which covers far more topics than your own tickets would
Questions the engineering team writes, since they know the product and its edge cases best
The model's own ratings of its past answers, which scale better than any human labelling

questions.explanation: Applied-llms.org recommends assertion-based tests built from real input and output samples. Real tickets carry the wording, typos and edge cases your users actually produce; invented or benchmark questions test something else. Assertions ("mentions the 30-day window", "doesn't promise a refund") make the evals checkable.

questions.prompt: You want an LLM judge to compare two prompt versions of the support agent. Which setup does applied-llms.org say tends to give more stable results?

choices.text: Score each reply on its own from 1 to 10, then compare the averages
Ask the model that wrote each reply to grade its own answer
Show the judge both replies to the same ticket and ask which is better
Have the judge rewrite each reply and measure how much it changed

questions.explanation: Applied-llms.org notes that pairwise comparisons tend to be more stable than asking a judge to score single outputs on a scale. Scores on a 1 to 10 scale drift and bunch together. Either way, check the judge against a sample of human labels before trusting it.

questions.prompt: Which rollout order is safest for the new support agent?

choices.text: Launch to all users at once, then fix whatever the complaints and ratings reveal
Offline evals, shadow mode on real traffic, a small share of users, then a monitored ramp-up
A small share of users first, then offline evals once there's real traffic to build them from
Offline evals, then straight to all users with monitoring, since passing evals shows it's ready

questions.explanation: Each stage catches problems the previous one can't: offline evals catch known failures, shadow mode shows behaviour on real inputs with no user impact, and a small share of real users limits the blast radius of what's left. Applied-llms.org's advice to build trust by starting small, and its shadow-pipeline idea for new models, both point to this order.

questions.prompt: Your provider releases a new version of the model your support agent uses. What does applied-llms.org recommend?

choices.text: Use the provider's "latest" alias so production upgrades automatically
Switch at once, because newer versions are always at least as good
Never upgrade, because any change risks breaking the agent
Pin the current version in production and test the new one in a shadow pipeline first

questions.explanation: Applied-llms.org says to version and pin your models so behaviour doesn't change under you, and to consider a shadow pipeline that mirrors production with the newer model to validate it before switching. A new version can be better overall and still break your prompts or output format.

questions.prompt: What would you monitor once the support agent is live, and what would make you roll back?

model_answer.summary: Track outcome, quality, cost and latency metrics plus a daily read of real transcripts, and roll back on a pre-agreed threshold such as a jump in handoffs, failed checks or complaints.
key_points: Outcome metrics: resolution rate, handoff rate and customer feedback
Quality signals: guardrail and output-check failure rates, and scores from online evals or an LLM judge on sampled conversations
Cost per conversation and latency per turn, from traces
Someone reads a sample of real conversations every day to spot new failure modes
A written rollback trigger (for example handoff rate or check failures above a set level after a release) and a quick way to return to the previous prompt or model version

questions.explanation: Applied-llms.org stresses looking at samples of inputs and outputs every day and watching for drift between development and production. Monitoring is only useful with a decision attached, which is why the rollback trigger belongs in the design.
